2.text: vaccination-boys were sent to inspect the population. They found that nearly

3.text: everybody had been vaccinated. Those that were not, were vaccinated this

4.text: time. Immediately after that, the small-pox came, and destroyed about one

5.text: third of the whole population. It proved afterwards that the vaccine sent

6.text: from Irkutsk sealed in small tubes was worthless, and the vaccination-boys

7.text: kept their lancets in such a state, that they were more suitable for inoculating

8.text: syphilis than for simple vaccination. Exactly the same occurrences were repeated

9.text: in 1889, at the second outbreak of the small-pox.

10.text: The first graduated physician visited the Kolyma in 1817. He was Dr.

11.text: Reslein, chief physician of the province of Yakutsk. He was, according to

12.text: Gedenstrom, one of the most charitable men of his time, but at the same

13.text: time he was of a quite eccentric character. He would receive no payment

14.text: or presents for his medical assistance. The greater part of his salary he left

15.text: in the Treasury, and took only as much as he thought necessary for his

16.text: scanty sustenance. Any cynic of modern times could hardly surpass him in

17.text: his mode of life. In the winter-time, during the most severe cold, he used

18.text: to wear summer clothes, a light uniform, a hat, rarely an overcoat of broadcloth.

19.text: In the year 1817 he received an order from the Government to send some

20.text: physician from Yakutsk to Zashiversk and Sredne-Kolymsk, on account of

21.text: syphilis and leprosy, which were ravaging those countries. Reslein, who was

22.text: about seventy years old, chose to go himself. He left Yakutsk in October,

23.text: notwithstanding the cold, clad in broadcloth. On the way he used to alight

24.text: from his horse, run about, or even turn somersaults, in order to keep himself

25.text: warm. In this way he made fifteen hundred versts, and then his feet were

26.text: frost-bitten. He was taken to Sredne-Kolymsk on a litter, wrapped in skins.

27.text: There he amputated several of his toes himself, and after six months he died.

28.text: He lies buried in Sredne-Kolymsk. He left a great number of manuscripts,

29.text: which came into possession of his heirs.¹

30.text: The strange fate of Dr. Reslein has served as the basis of a tale, which

31.text: I collected on the Lower Kolyma. The old doctor is described as a young

32.text: courtier of very high blood, who was sent to the Kolyma for political reasons,

33.text: and preferred to destroy his own life. “The Kolyma is not worthy of such

34.text: a man,” he would say before his death. All this, of course, is pure fiction.

35.text: Since this first medical visit of Reslein, I am aware of but one other

36.text: graduated surgeon, Dr. Nekrasov, who lived in the Kolyma district during

37.text: the seventies of the nineteenth century, and died there. Another one came

38.text: during our stay in the early nineties. He seemed not to be in his full mental

39.text: health, and had to leave very soon. In the last years of the nineteenth

40.text: century, Dr. Mitzkevich, a political exile to one of the southern districts of

41.text: the Yakutsk Province, proposed to go to the Kolyma as a district surgeon,

42.text: and was allowed to do so. When his term of exile expired, he was replaced
